parts.title: Problem Solving — A water leak in the condo

texts.text:
Nadia: Hi, is this Greg? It's Nadia Rahimi in unit 1204. I'm sorry to call so early, but there's water coming through my bathroom ceiling.
Greg: Good morning, Nadia. No problem, that's what I'm here for. How much water are we talking about?
Nadia: It's a steady drip, maybe one drop every second, right above the bathtub. There's a brown stain about the size of a dinner plate, and it seems to be getting bigger.
Greg: Okay. Above the tub is actually the best place for it, because the water's going straight down the drain. Is the ceiling sagging at all, like it's bulging down?
Nadia: No, it's flat. Just wet.
Greg: Good. Then it's probably not dangerous. The unit above you is 1304. The owners are away in Portugal until the end of the month, but I have a key. Most likely it's their bathtub or the toilet supply line. I'll go up there right now and check.
Nadia: Thank you. I have to leave for work at eight-thirty, though.
Greg: That's fine. You don't need to be home for me to get into 1304.

Greg: Nadia, it's Greg again. I found it. The pipe that feeds the toilet in 1304 had a crack in it, so water was spraying behind the toilet and soaking into the floor. I've turned off the water to that toilet, so the leak should stop within the hour once the floor dries out a bit.
Nadia: That's a relief. What about my ceiling, though? The stain's pretty ugly.
Greg: The drywall will need to dry completely first. If we paint it too early, the stain just comes back through the paint. I'll bring you a fan this evening to speed things up. Give it about a week.
Nadia: And who pays for the repair? I don't want this coming out of my pocket.
Greg: In a case like this, it usually goes through the building's insurance, because the pipe failed on its own. Nobody did anything wrong. But there's a deductible, and the condo board decides how that's shared. I'll put it on the agenda for the next meeting.

Nadia: Greg, one more thing. My bathroom fan has been making a rattling noise for weeks. While someone's here, could they look at that too?
Greg: Sure, but just so you know, the fan is inside your unit, so it's your responsibility, not the building's. I can give you the name of the electrician we use. He charges about ninety dollars to come out.
Nadia: Ninety dollars just to show up?
Greg: That includes the first half hour. Honestly, it's often just dust in the motor. Try cleaning the cover with a vacuum first. If it's still rattling after that, give him a call.
Nadia: Okay, I'll try that tonight. Thanks for being so quick this morning.
Greg: No problem. I'll drop the fan off around six.

parts.title: Information — Getting a fishing licence

texts.text:
Caller: Hi, I'm planning to take my two kids fishing at Pine Lake next month, and I'm not sure what licences we need.
Officer: Happy to help. How old are the children?
Caller: Eight and thirteen.
Officer: Then they don't need anything. In this province, anyone under sixteen can fish without a licence, as long as they're with an adult who has one. So it's just you.
Caller: Great. Where do I get it?
Officer: Almost everyone buys it online now. It takes about ten minutes. You'll need a valid ID, and you'll have to print the licence or keep it on your phone. Officers can ask to see it at any time.
Caller: What does it cost?
Officer: An annual licence for a resident is twenty-eight dollars. If you only fish once or twice a year, there's also a one-day licence for twelve, but if you're going more than twice, the annual one is better value.
Caller: We'll probably go three or four times this summer.
Officer: Then the annual licence makes sense. One more thing: Pine Lake has special rules. You can keep up to four walleye a day, but any walleye longer than fifty centimetres has to go back in the water. Those are the big breeding fish.
Caller: How would I know how long it is?
Officer: Most people bring a measuring tape. There's also a measuring board on the dock at the boat launch.
Caller: Good to know. Can we use live minnows as bait?
Officer: Not at Pine Lake. Live bait fish are banned there to keep other species out of the lake. Worms are fine, though, and so are lures.

parts.title: News Item — A library lends out more than books

texts.text:
Reporter: Residents of Lakeview who need a power drill, a sewing machine or even a telescope no longer have to buy one. Starting next Monday, the Lakeview Public Library will open what it calls a "Library of Things" at its Main Street branch.
The new collection includes more than two hundred items, from camping stoves and snowshoes to board games and a professional-quality camera. Anyone with a free library card can borrow up to two items at a time for one week.
Head librarian Marisa Coelho says the idea came from the library's own survey last year, in which many residents said they wanted to try a hobby but could not afford the equipment. "Most people use a drill for maybe fifteen minutes in its whole life," she said. "It makes more sense for a community to share one."
The project cost about forty thousand dollars, most of it paid by a provincial grant for programs that reduce waste. Local businesses donated some of the larger items, including a pressure washer and two kayaks.
Late fees will not apply, but borrowers who damage an item will be asked to pay for repairs. The library says it plans to add more items in the spring, based on requests from users.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should cities stop mowing some of their parks?

texts.text:
Speaker: Drive through almost any Canadian city in summer and you'll see the same thing: neat, short grass in every park, along every boulevard and around every highway ramp. Keeping it that way costs a fortune. Some cities spend millions of dollars a year on mowing, and the mowers themselves burn a surprising amount of fuel.
That's why a growing number of municipalities are trying something called "naturalization". Instead of mowing everything, they let selected areas grow long, sometimes planting native wildflowers and grasses. Supporters point out three benefits. First, it saves money and fuel. Second, longer grass and wildflowers give bees and butterflies the food and shelter they've been losing. And third, deep-rooted native plants soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding after storms.
Not everyone is convinced. Some residents complain that unmowed areas look messy, like the city has simply given up. Others worry about ticks, which can carry Lyme disease and tend to live in long grass. Those are real concerns, and I don't think cities should dismiss them.
But I think the answer lies in where and how it's done. Nobody is suggesting we stop mowing soccer fields or the lawn beside the playground. The best programs keep a mown strip along every path, so people can walk without brushing against long grass, and they put up signs explaining what's being grown and why. When people understand that the long grass is a choice, not neglect, most of the complaints disappear.
So my view is this: cities should naturalize the places where people rarely walk, such as highway ramps, steep slopes and the far edges of large parks, and keep mowing the places where people actually play.

Arjun: Hi, I was booked on the 6:40 flight to Winnipeg tonight, and the board just says "cancelled". Can you tell me what's going on?

Agent: Thank you. I can put you on the first flight tomorrow morning, which leaves at 7:15 and lands at 9:05. Or there's a flight tonight through Calgary, but you'd land in Winnipeg at 1:30 in the morning.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should newcomers buy a car right away?

texts.text:
Speaker: One of the first questions many newcomers to Canada ask me is, "Should I buy a car?" It's an understandable question. In much of the country, distances are large, winters are hard, and public transit outside the big cities can be limited. A car can feel like the key to freedom.
But my advice, in most cases, is to wait at least a few months. Here's why.
First, the cost is much higher than people expect. It isn't just the price of the car. Insurance for a new driver with no Canadian driving history can cost several hundred dollars a month, sometimes more than the car payment itself. Add gas, winter tires, parking and repairs, and many families are surprised by the total.
Second, many newcomers can't use their foreign licence for long. In most provinces, you can drive on it for a limited time, usually a few months, and then you must pass Canadian tests. If you buy a car first, you may end up paying for it while you wait for a road test.
Third, you don't yet know where you'll live or work. Many people move apartments or change jobs in their first year. A car that seemed essential for one commute may be unnecessary after the next move.
That said, I'm not against cars. In small towns or for shift workers whose jobs start before the buses run, a car may be necessary from day one. My point is simply that it shouldn't be an automatic decision. Try transit, car-sharing and carpooling first. Get your licence sorted out. Then, if you still need a car, you'll be in a much better position to choose one.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Is tipping still a good system?

texts.text:
Speaker: A few years ago, I tipped when someone served me a meal at a table, and that was about it. Today, I'm asked to tip almost everywhere: at the coffee counter, at the self-checkout of a frozen yogurt shop, even when I pick up a takeout order myself. The payment screen turns toward me with options of eighteen, twenty or twenty-five percent, and I feel the cashier watching.
Many Canadians feel the same way. Surveys show that most people think tipping has gotten out of hand. And yet most of us keep tipping, partly out of habit and partly because we know that service workers don't earn much.
That second reason is the heart of the problem. In many workplaces, tips aren't really a reward for excellent service. They're part of how the business pays its staff. The customer, in effect, is asked to cover part of the wage that the employer chooses not to pay.
Some restaurants in Canada have tried a different model. They raise their menu prices by about fifteen percent, pay staff a better hourly wage, and tell customers that no tip is expected. The results have been mixed. Staff often earn more reliable income, but some customers see the higher prices and go elsewhere, not realizing that the final bill is about the same.
I don't think we should abolish tipping overnight. Many workers depend on it, and they could lose income if it disappeared without a plan. But I'd like to see two changes. First, tip screens should start with a "no tip" option that isn't hidden. Second, more businesses should include fair wages in their prices and say so clearly. Then a tip could go back to being what it was meant to be: a thank-you for great service, not a hidden part of the bill.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should high-school students do volunteer hours?

texts.text:
Speaker: In Ontario, high-school students must complete forty hours of community service before they can graduate. Some other provinces have no such rule, and every few years someone asks whether all of Canada should require it. As a former teacher, I've watched this program up close, and I have mixed feelings.
On the positive side, I've seen students discover things about themselves they never would have found in a classroom. A shy girl who volunteered at a seniors' home became so confident that she later studied nursing. A boy who helped coach a children's soccer team realized he wanted to be a teacher. For some students, those forty hours open a door.
But for many others, I'm afraid the hours are just a box to tick. In the spring of grade twelve, students scramble to find any activity that counts, and some organizations sign the forms without checking how much work was really done. When volunteering is forced and rushed, students don't learn generosity. They learn to see helping others as a chore.
There's also a fairness issue. Students who work part-time jobs to support their families, or who look after younger siblings, have much less free time. Yet their responsibilities don't count as community service.
So here is what I'd suggest. Keep the requirement, but make it more meaningful. Spread the hours over all four years instead of letting them pile up at the end. Let schools count family caregiving and some paid work in special cases. And ask students to write a short reflection about what they learned. Forty hours can be valuable, but only if students have the time and the reason to take them seriously.

parts.title: Viewpoints — The value of learning a trade

texts.text:
Speaker: For years, high-school students in Canada have been told the same thing: to succeed, go to university. Parents push for it, guidance offices are organized around it, and students who choose a trade, like plumbing, electrical work or welding, are sometimes treated as if they've settled for less.
I think that message has done real damage, and I'm glad it's finally changing.
Consider the job market. Canada faces a serious shortage of skilled tradespeople. Many experienced workers are retiring, and there aren't enough young people to replace them. As a result, a licensed electrician or plumber can often earn as much as, or more than, many university graduates, and they usually start earning much earlier.
There's also the question of debt. A four-year degree can leave a student owing tens of thousands of dollars. In most trades, apprentices are paid while they learn. They spend most of their time working on real job sites and only a few weeks a year in a classroom, so many finish their training with little or no debt.
I want to be fair. Trades are physically demanding, and not every job is steady; some construction work slows down in winter. And university remains the right path for people who want to become doctors, engineers or teachers.
My point is not that trades are better than university. It's that they deserve equal respect. Schools should introduce students to the trades early, through workshops and job-shadowing, so that young people can choose based on their interests, not on old ideas about which jobs are "good enough".

Thank you for your email asking whether our neighbourhood could have an outdoor skating rink in Kildonan Park again this winter. I am happy to tell you that the answer is yes, although the rink will look a little different from the one you remember.

parts.title: Information — The return of the swift fox

texts.text: The swift fox is the smallest wild dog in North America, about the size of a house cat. It once lived across the grasslands of the Prairies, from southern Alberta to Manitoba. By the late 1930s, however, it had completely disappeared from Canada. Hunting, trapping and poison meant for wolves all played a part, but the biggest cause was the loss of its home, as wild grassland was ploughed into farmland.

In 1983, a small group of researchers and volunteers began trying to bring the fox back. They used foxes born in captivity, mainly at a centre near Cochrane, Alberta, and others brought from the United States. Over the next fourteen years, more than nine hundred foxes were released in southern Alberta and Saskatchewan. Many did not survive their first winter, often because they were caught by coyotes or golden eagles.

Slowly, however, the foxes that survived began to have their own young in the wild. Surveys in the 2000s found a few hundred swift foxes living in the border region between Canada and the United States, and the population has grown since then. In 2012, the swift fox's status in Canada was changed from "endangered" to "threatened", which means it is still at risk but no longer close to disappearing.

Today, scientists believe the main threats are vehicles on rural roads and the continued loss of grassland. Because swift foxes spend most of the day in underground dens and hunt at night, they are rarely seen by people. Ranchers have become important partners, because cattle grazing keeps the grass short, which the foxes prefer for spotting danger.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should cities ban gas-powered leaf blowers?

texts.text:
Every fall, the quiet of my street is broken by the high, angry whine of gas-powered leaf blowers. Several Canadian cities are now considering banning them, and I think it is time we did.
The first argument is noise. Gas blowers are extraordinarily loud, often between seventy and ninety decibels at the operator's ear, and their low-frequency rumble travels through walls and windows. For people who work from home, care for babies, or work night shifts, an hour of blowing next door is more than an annoyance; it is a real disruption to their lives and their health.
The second argument is pollution. Most gas blowers use small two-stroke engines, which burn a mix of gas and oil and are far dirtier than a car engine. Studies in the United States have found that one hour with a commercial leaf blower can produce as much of certain pollutants as driving a car hundreds of kilometres. The workers who use them every day breathe that exhaust at close range.
Critics of a ban argue that landscaping companies need these machines to work quickly, and that a ban would raise the cost of their services. This is a fair concern. But battery-powered blowers have improved enormously in the past five years. They are much quieter, produce no exhaust, and are now powerful enough for most residential work. Cities that have introduced bans, such as Montreal's borough of Rosemont, have usually given businesses two or three years to switch, and some have offered rebates to help cover the cost of new equipment.
I am not asking anyone to rake every leaf by hand, although many of us could use the exercise. I am asking cities to phase out a machine whose costs are paid by everyone except the person using it.

I agree with this article, though I think the writer is a little hard on landscapers. My brother runs a small landscaping company, and he switched to battery blowers last year. He says they are [1] than the old ones, and his clients love it. The batteries were [2], though. He spent almost three thousand dollars on new equipment, so I support the idea of [3] for small businesses.
What I don't agree with is the idea of raking by hand. With [4] in my backyard, raking takes me a whole weekend, and I'm sixty-eight. A ban should give people like me enough [5] to buy a quiet battery model before it starts.

parts.title: Information — The story of Canada's first ice-cream truck route

texts.text: In the hot summer of 1952, a Winnipeg milkman named Harold Petrie had an idea. His horse-drawn milk deliveries ended by noon, and his small refrigerated wagon sat empty for the rest of the day. Why not fill it with ice cream and sell it in the afternoons? With a loan of three hundred dollars from his brother, he bought a freezer that ran on a car battery and painted the wagon bright yellow.

The first week was a disaster. Petrie drove through the city's business district, where office workers had no time to stop. Then his daughter suggested trying the new suburbs, where young families were moving in large numbers. There, children ran out of every house when they heard him coming, and within a month he had sold more ice cream than milk.

The bell that made him famous came by accident. When his wagon's old bell broke, Petrie borrowed a small brass bell from a school. Its bright, clear sound carried much farther than the old one, and parents began to call it "the Petrie bell". Other sellers soon copied it, and by the end of the decade, bells and later recorded music became the signal of ice cream across the country.

Petrie sold his business in 1971, by which time it had grown to fourteen trucks. He always said his greatest pride was not the money but the jobs it gave to students, many of whom drove his trucks to pay for university. A small museum in St. Boniface displays one of his original yellow wagons today.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should children walk to school alone?

texts.text:
When I was eight, I walked to school by myself every day: twelve minutes, two quiet streets and one crossing with a guard. Today, on my street in Calgary, I almost never see a child under twelve walking alone. Most are driven, even when the school is less than a kilometre away. I think we have gone too far in protecting our children from the world.
Parents usually give two reasons for driving: traffic and strangers. Traffic is a real danger, and I would never send a young child alone along a busy road. But the fear of strangers is greatly out of proportion to the actual risk. Crimes against children by strangers are extremely rare in Canada, and they have not become more common since my childhood. What has changed is how much we hear about them.
Meanwhile, the costs of driving everywhere are real. Children who walk to school get exercise before they sit at a desk for six hours, and teachers often say these students arrive more alert. Walking alone also teaches independence: reading the street, judging when to cross, solving small problems without an adult. These are skills children need before they become teenagers, not after.
Ironically, the crowds of parents' cars around schools at 8:30 have made the streets more dangerous for the few children who do walk.
I am not suggesting that every child should walk alone at six. Parents know their children and their neighbourhoods. But we could start small: walking with a group of friends, walking alone for the last block, or setting up "walking school buses", where one adult walks a group of children along a fixed route. Freedom, like any skill, can be learned in steps.

That said, I love the idea of the walking school bus. Our neighbourhood started one last fall, and it has [4]. Five parents take turns, so each of us only walks one morning a week. My son, who used to complain about the walk, now [5] because his friends are there.

parts.title: Information — The Halifax Explosion

texts.text: On the morning of December 6, 1917, two ships collided in the narrow channel of Halifax Harbour. One of them, the French cargo ship Mont-Blanc, was carrying nearly three thousand tonnes of explosives for the war in Europe. A fire broke out on board, and the crew, knowing what was in the hold, abandoned ship and rowed to the opposite shore. About twenty minutes later, the burning ship drifted against a pier and exploded.

The blast was the largest human-made explosion in history before the atomic bomb. It destroyed much of the north end of the city, killed about two thousand people and injured around nine thousand. Windows shattered more than eighty kilometres away. Many of the injuries were to people's eyes, because crowds had gathered at their windows to watch the burning ship.

Help arrived quickly. Within hours, trains carrying doctors, nurses and supplies left for Halifax from across the Maritimes. The most famous help came from Boston, where officials sent a relief train with medical teams and supplies, even though a blizzard the next day slowed it down. Each year since 1971, Nova Scotia has sent a large Christmas tree to Boston to say thank you.

The disaster also led to lasting changes. Halifax was rebuilt with new housing, including the Hydrostone district, whose homes were built from fire-resistant concrete blocks. The great number of eye injuries helped lead to improvements in eye care in Canada and to the founding of what later became the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Is it time to end daylight saving time?

texts.text:
Twice a year, most Canadians change their clocks: forward one hour in March, back one hour in November. The idea, which became common during the First World War, was to save energy by making better use of daylight in the evenings. More than a century later, I believe the practice has outlived its purpose.
The energy argument no longer holds. Studies in several countries have found that the savings from daylight saving time are tiny or non-existent today, because modern homes use energy for heating, air conditioning and electronics regardless of what time the sun sets.
Meanwhile, the costs are well documented. In the days after the spring change, when we lose an hour of sleep, researchers have recorded increases in traffic accidents, workplace injuries and even heart attacks. Parents of young children will also tell you that it can take a week or more for a toddler's sleep schedule to recover.
Most people agree on ending the switch. The real debate is about which time to keep. Many people prefer permanent daylight time, which would give us light later in the evenings all year. But sleep scientists strongly prefer permanent standard time, because it keeps the clock closer to the sun. With permanent daylight time, winter sunrise in many Canadian cities would come after nine in the morning, meaning children would travel to school in the dark for months.
Some provinces have passed laws to adopt permanent daylight time, but only if neighbouring provinces and American states do the same, so that business and travel are not disrupted. I understand that caution. Still, I would encourage our governments to choose permanent standard time, and to act together soon. The twice-yearly switch helps no one.

In summer, permanent daylight time would give me [2] after work to enjoy with my kids. Dark winter mornings are a [3] price, in my opinion, because winter mornings are dark here anyway.
I also think the writer is [4] about the provinces waiting for their neighbours. If we wait for everyone to agree, we will [5] be changing our clocks in fifty years.

parts.title: Information — Saving the Garry oak meadows

texts.text: Garry oak meadows are one of the rarest ecosystems in Canada. They grow only in a small area of southeastern Vancouver Island, a few of the Gulf Islands and one spot in the Fraser Valley. In spring, they are covered in wildflowers such as camas lilies, whose blue flowers once stretched across hills that are now covered by houses and roads in and around Victoria.

For thousands of years before European settlement, the Lekwungen and other Coast Salish peoples looked after these meadows. They harvested camas bulbs as an important food and used controlled fires to keep shrubs and young trees from taking over. Without these fires, many meadows slowly turned into forest after settlement.

Today, less than five percent of the original Garry oak meadows remain in a natural condition. The biggest threats are city development and invasive plants such as Scotch broom and English ivy, which grow quickly and crowd out native species. More than one hundred plants and animals that live in these meadows are considered at risk.

Many groups are working to protect what is left. Volunteers spend weekends pulling Scotch broom by hand, and some homeowners in Victoria have replaced their lawns with native meadow plants. In recent years, several First Nations have also worked with parks staff to bring back traditional practices, including small controlled burns and camas harvesting, which help the meadows stay healthy.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should restaurants post calorie counts?

texts.text:
Since 2017, large restaurant chains in Ontario have been required to show the number of calories next to each item on their menus. Other provinces are now considering similar laws. Supporters say it helps people make healthier choices; critics say it does little good and may even cause harm. Having looked at the evidence, I find myself somewhere in the middle.
The case for calorie labels is simple: information is power. Most of us greatly underestimate how much energy is in restaurant food. A muffin that looks like a light breakfast can contain more calories than a hamburger. Without labels, customers cannot make an informed choice, even if they want to.
But does the information change behaviour? Here the research is mixed. Several studies have found that customers order slightly fewer calories when labels are present, often around five to ten percent less per meal. That is not nothing, but it is not a revolution either. Interestingly, some of the biggest changes have come from the restaurants themselves. Faced with publishing embarrassing numbers, many chains quietly reduced portion sizes or changed recipes.
Critics raise a serious concern about people with eating disorders, for whom calorie numbers can trigger anxiety and unhealthy behaviour. This deserves to be taken seriously. One solution, used in some places, is to offer menus without calorie information on request.
There is also a question of what calories leave out. A small bag of chips and a bowl of lentil soup may have similar calories, but very different nutrition. Some experts suggest adding simple symbols for salt or sugar.
My conclusion: calorie labels are a useful but modest tool. They are worth keeping, but we should not expect them alone to solve our health problems.

parts.title: Information — Canada's first female doctor

texts.text: Emily Stowe was born in 1831 in what is now Ontario. As a young woman, she trained as a teacher and in 1852 became the first female principal of a public school in Upper Canada. But after her husband became ill with tuberculosis, she decided she wanted to study medicine, a field that was closed to women in Canada at the time.

When she applied to the Toronto School of Medicine, she was refused. The vice-president of the university reportedly told her that its doors were not open to women and, he hoped, never would be. Determined, Stowe went to the United States and in 1867 graduated from the New York Medical College for Women. She returned to Toronto and opened a medical practice, although without a Canadian licence.

Practising medicine without a licence was risky, and in 1879 she was taken to court after one of her patients died. She was found not guilty, and the case brought her a great deal of public attention. In 1880, she was finally granted a licence to practise in Canada. Meanwhile, her daughter, Augusta Stowe-Gullen, became the first woman to earn a medical degree in Canada, in 1883.

Stowe spent the rest of her life fighting for women's rights. In 1876, she had founded the Toronto Women's Literary Club, which was really a group working for women's right to vote. She also helped to establish the Woman's Medical College in Toronto, so that other women would not have to leave the country to study medicine as she had done.

parts.title: Viewpoints — Should grocery stores end self-checkout?

texts.text:
A few years ago, self-checkout machines seemed like the future of shopping. Today, some stores in North America are quietly removing them, and I think they are right to reconsider.
The machines were supposed to save time and money. For shoppers with only a few items, they often do. But for a full cart of groceries, they can be slower than a trained cashier, especially when customers have to weigh vegetables, look up product codes and call for help every time the machine announces an "unexpected item in the bagging area". Many shoppers now complain that they have been turned into unpaid store employees.
Stores have also discovered a hidden cost: theft. Several large retailers have reported that losses from self-checkout are much higher than from staffed lanes. Some of this is deliberate stealing, but much of it is honest mistakes, such as items that are scanned wrongly or not at all.
There is also a human cost. For many older customers, people with disabilities and newcomers who are still learning English, a cashier is not just someone who scans food. A friendly conversation at the checkout may be one of the few social moments in their day.
I am not calling for a total ban. Self-checkout can work well as one option among several, for people with a basket of a few items. But stores should never force customers to use it by closing staffed lanes. The best solution is a balance: keep enough cashiers so that nobody has to wait long, and let customers choose.

I do think the writer is a little [4] on the machines, though. On a busy Saturday, I see many young customers who are [5] to use self-checkout for a few items and avoid waiting.
